title: Remember, remember
hookLine: raam simar raam simar ihai tero kaaj hai: remember, this is your real work (Jaijavanti M9, ang 1352)

lines: ONE LINE WRITTEN AT THE TOP.
cards: A to-do list on a Monday morning. Reply to the landlord. Book the dentist.
Finish the report. Buy milk. Call Mom back.
Return the package. It's long, and everything on it feels urgent. Now imagine someone gently taking the pen and writing one more line at the very top, above all of it, underlined twice.
Not instead of the list. Above it. Guru Tegh Bahadur's hymn in Raag Jaijavanti does exactly that.

teach.b: The hymn opens raam simar, raam simar, ihai tero kaaj hai. Remember the Lord, remember the Lord: this is your work. Simar is the root of simran: remembering, keeping the Lord in mind, often by repeating the Name.
Raam, in Gurbani, is the all-pervading One.

teach.h: KAAJ: THE JOB YOU CAME TO DO.
teach.b: And kaaj is work, the job you came to do. Why say it twice? Think of how you call someone who's drifting off: hey, hey.
The doubling is a hand on the shoulder. Then, in paraphrase: leave the company of maya, and take shelter with the Lord. Know the world's pleasures to be false; all this show is passing.

teach.h: WEALTH AS A DREAM, A WALL OF SAND.
teach.b: Know wealth as a dream; why be proud of it? The kingdom of the whole earth is like a wall of sand. And near the end, Nanak says the body will perish, as time slips away moment by moment.

teach.h: THE WORK UNDER ALL THE WORK.
teach.b: The hymn doesn't call remembering a hobby, or a reward for when the work is done. It calls it the work.
Sikhs hear the same thought in a hymn of Guru Arjan's in the evening prayer: no other task will help you; join the holy company and meditate on the Name alone. So the list doesn't vanish.
You still buy the milk and call your mother. But the line at the top changes the rest, because the other jobs no longer carry your whole worth.
That's simran: the work under all the work.

how: Many Sikhs begin the day with simran, repeating Waheguru, before Nitnem and the day's work; Guru Tegh Bahadur's Jaijavanti shabad 'raam simar raam simar' is sung in kirtan as a call to that practice.

o: keeping the Lord in mind, simran
recalling the days of one's past

p: work, the task you came to do

s: the hymn calls remembering a reward for when the work is done
it calls remembering the work itself: ihai tero kaaj hai.
the hymn says the opening call twice
raam simar, raam simar: a nudge, a hand on the shoulder.
the hymn says to drop all ordinary duties
the list stays; remembering goes at the top and makes the rest lighter.

games.q: your to-do list is long and urgent. what does the Jaijavanti hymn say is your real work?
games.why: raam simar, raam simar, ihai tero kaaj hai: remember the Lord, remember: this is your work.

practice: Before the list, the phone or the inbox, sit and breathe slowly.

If you pray, repeat Waheguru quietly, once on each breath, the way Sikhs practice simran; if you don't, come back again and again to the plain fact that you're here and alive. When the list starts calling, let it wait.

wordCard.voice: Remember. Raam simar, raam simar: Guru Tegh Bahadur says twice that remembering the Lord is your real work, the job under every other job.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: simran, remembering, from the same root as the hymn's simar.

carryVoice: Your line: this is your work. The list still gets done; it just isn't at the top. Day five hundred eighty-five, done.

sources.ref: Raag Jaijavanti, Mahalla 9, 'raam simar raam simar ihai tero kaaj hai' (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1352)
Raag Asa, Mahalla 5, 'avar kaaj terai kitai na kaam' (Rehras; Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 12)
